text: Evening, all. One man on the Wall road between Clark and Rich, one in a boat between Silke and Paddy. I'll be fair and tell you now that the first one I ride on is Clark. As for tax, Reina, darling, you'll get my tax the day you can come and collect it.

Rob, darling, a man who rides the Wall road ought to read the stars too. I name you keeper of the I Ching, so shuffle honestly, and there may be a scholar's salary in it at year's end. Clark, don't look so pale, I haven't forgotten you.
Reina appoints Rob to read the I Ching and keep the population counter, from Year 2; his Scholar's salary of 5 is hers to decide each year. Rob shuffles the deck.

Silke, Paddy, my dears, just the customary five apiece, the smallest rent in the Middle Kingdom, and the Harvest Pile pays you back many times over. Your Majesty, the gentry of the north-west are, as ever, your most humble servants. Rob, if you're riding on Clark first, I'll keep a lamp lit for him.
Rent: Silke and Paddy each pay Rich 5.

A gentle thirty percent this year, friends, so twelve from each of you, and nobody can call that greed. The Summer Palace goes up first, since every wall and every canal starts there. Clark gets his five for collecting, and Rob, the scholar's five is yours as long as the stars come out honest and Clark stays on his feet.
Tax at 30% on this year's 60 is 18 from each province, not 12: 72 in all from Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy. Rob has refused his.

Thirty percent is eighteen a head, friends, not twelve. Her Majesty's arithmetic is generous, but the crown's ledger isn't. Eighteen from me, eighteen from Rich, Silke and Paddy, and seventy-two goes to the treasury. Rob, your refusal is now on the books in my best hand, with the date. And Rob, the man you say you'll ride on first happens to be the man who knows where everybody's grain is kept. You might think twice about that.
Clark collects 18 each from Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy: 72 to the crown. Rob refuses his. Reina builds the Summer Palace on G26, the far eastern corner of Province 1, for 20 from the crown.

My Customs House opens at four, friends, and every merchant on the Wall road will be glad of it. I'm bidding on all three of the rest. I keep the receipts, so a man with the books in his hands can't be outbid for long. Rich, if you're thinking of collecting the whole set, remember who tallies your Harvest Pile.

Friends, I'll be a modest bidder tonight. A gentleman doesn't fight over crockery, and every grain we throw at each other just ends up in the Pile. My Land Deed goes up at three, a fair price for good earth. Clark, dear fellow, I'll only say this: I'd hate to see you overpay for a jar.

Rent five, tax eighteen, and I'm sitting on thirty-seven, same as Paddy. So nobody at this table gets to call either of us rich tonight. Clark, Rich, I'm bidding on your Customs House and your Land Deed, and I'm bidding honestly. Paddy, keep your Bowl's price down where friends can reach it, and maybe I'll keep the Jar cheap for you too.

Well now, there's two of everything, so there's no call for any of us to be clawing at each other. I'll put a fair few grains on each piece and not a grain past fair, and my Wooden Bowl goes up at two, honest as the rice it holds. Silke, love, you and I want the same things, so let's not make Rich's Harvest Pile rich on our account.

Keeper of the I Ching, how lovely, Reina. I'll shuffle as honestly as I ride. No bids from me, friends: you buy the pretty things and set them out on the board, and I'll come round later and admire them up close. Clark, put the date on that too.

The auctions: Silke wins Clark's Customs House at 9 (Rich and Paddy stop at 8) and Rich's Land Deed Scroll at 9 (Clark stops at 7, Paddy at 8). Rich wins Silke's Dragon Jar at 10 (Paddy stops at 8, Clark at 9) and Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 10 (Silke stops at 7, Clark at 9). Rob bids on nothing.

Nine and nine, Clark, Rich, and I'll take your receipts. That's two of my three, and Rich paid ten for my Jar, so a quarter of that comes back to the silk coast. Paddy, love, you stopped at eight both times. I did notice.

Silke, Paddy, your lovely things will sit in the quietest corner of the north-west, safe as heirlooms. Rob, you're welcome to come and admire them, but it's a long ride for a short look. And Clark, do write it down: two pieces, twenty grain, paid in full.
Silke places the Customs House on L24 and the Land Deed Scroll on M24; Rich places the Dragon Jar on L12 and the Wooden Bowl on M13.

Rich, you said it was a long ride for a short look, so I've started early. That's five from the north-west, and five from you too, Silke, for the sea air. Clark, I haven't forgotten you, I'm just going the scenic way. And look, a third man's camped under Paddy's rice paddies. Shuffle up, everyone, Year 2 is going to be lively.

Rob's W1 steps onto H10 and W2 onto P25: 5 from Rich and 5 from Silke. Rob hires a third soldier, W3, on T21 below Paddy's province, for 20 to the pile; his army is full at three. Salaries: Reina pays Clark 5 and Rob 5.
Rob reads the I Ching as Reina's appointee, not as Scholar: his 5 a year is hers to choose at salaries, not owed.

Gather round, children, and hear the stars, shuffled honestly as promised. "Spring Floods. Heaven waters the land generously. In some places, far too generously." Good harvests in 1, 3, 6 and 7, so well done Reina, Rich and Paddy. Bad harvests in 2, 4, 5 and 8, which means Clark, Silke, and my own poor desert. The population holds at 100 million, multiple x1, so read your first row. Clark, Silke, my condolences. Hungry neighbours make for very interesting neighbours.
Harvest (Spring Floods, x1): Reina +40, Rich +60, Paddy +60, Clark +10, Silke +10, Rob 0.

The floods were kind to some of us and cruel to others, so the harvest goes out exactly as the stars wrote it, to the last grain. Rent stays at the humble five. Silke, my dear, I won't squeeze a coast that's already been raided. Rob, you're a terrible guest, but at least you're a punctual one.
Rent: Silke and Paddy each pay Rich 5.

Clark is quite right, eighteen a head, and thank heaven one of us can count. Thirty percent again, friends, so Clark and Silke owe only three after the floods. The canal goes through my province this year, both sections, and the crown pays every grain of it. Rob, your five stands, but a scholar who raids the gentry reads a rather short almanac.
Reina declares 30% again: Clark 3, Silke 3, Rich 18, Paddy 18, 42 in all. She'll dig both sections of the Province 1 canal from the crown's grain (80), and pay Clark 5 and Rob 5 at the year's end.

Three from me, three from Silke, eighteen each from Rich and Paddy, and forty-two to the crown, all counted twice. Thank you, Your Majesty. It's nice to be right in public. Rob, that's your second refusal, and the page is filling up. Rich, you wanted it written down, so here it is: twenty grain for two pieces, five lost to a raider, sixty in from the floods, and both your heirlooms sitting in the north-west where anyone can see them.

"L12 and M13. Rich's Jar and Bowl are sitting there with nobody guarding them. Take them off the board before he finds a Land Deed, and next year the Official counts your tax refusal as a clerical oversight."
Rich needs a Customs House to finish his set, not a Land Deed: the Land Deed is his own province's realia.
Rich needs a Customs House to finish his set, not a Land Deed: the Land Deed is his own province's realia.

Clark collects 42: 3 each from Clark and Silke, 18 each from Rich and Paddy. Rob refuses his. Reina digs both sections of the Province 1 Grand Canal for 80 from the crown; they add 20 to her harvest from next year.

Correction noted, Storyteller, and noted in the book as well. Rich, it turns out the piece you're short of is mine, the very last Customs House in the kingdom, and it opens at twenty. A gentleman doesn't fight over crockery, you said, so this is your chance to prove it. Paddy, you and I want the same Deed and the same Jar, and there's one of each left. Bid high if you like, but I keep the receipts on everyone.

Your Majesty, a canal through your own province, how splendid; may it carry nothing but tribute. I'll be bidding on one piece only tonight, Clark's lovely Customs House, and I'll leave the crockery to those who still need it. My last Land Deed is the last one in the stock, though, so it goes up at twenty. Good earth is worth what it's worth.

Bad harvest, a raid, rent and tax, and I'm down to eighteen and a half. Clark, you've got fifty-six and three pieces still to buy, and I need exactly one, the last Bowl in the Kingdom. Stand aside on it and the silk coast backs you on whatever you need next, in public, starting now. Fight me on it and you'll pay every grain I have, and three quarters of that goes to Rich's Pile.

Right, I'll be plain with you all, since it's the last of each piece: I stopped at eight last year and I've had a whole flood season to regret it. The rice came in well, and I mean to bid like a man who'd like to be invited upstairs someday. Silke, love, my Bowl goes up at two, like I promised, so it's in reach of an honest pocket.

Rich, I'll confess something, because I'm a villain and not a sneak. A little bird with very neat handwriting has told me exactly where your Jar and Bowl are sitting, and he offered to lose my tax refusals in exchange. I'll be riding there anyway, Clark, so you can keep your clerical oversight. And none of you finishes your set while I'm still at the table.

The auctions: Rich wins Clark's last Customs House at 26 (Paddy stops at 25). Paddy wins Rich's last Land Deed Scroll at its minimum of 20, the only bid, and Silke's last Dragon Jar at 15 (Clark stops at 14). Silke wins Paddy's last Wooden Bowl at 9 (Clark stops at 8). Every province's stock is now sold.
There are two Customs Houses on the board: Rich's (just bought) and Silke's on L24, bought in Year 1.

Twenty-six grain, Clark, and worth every one. Your Customs House will sit in the north-west like a guest of honour. Paddy, you bid like a gentleman, and I don't forget a gentleman. Rob, I'm touched that you'd ride so far to see my little collection, but do mind the neat handwriting. Some clerks sell their maps to anybody.

Well, would you look at that, a rice farmer with a deed and a jar. I'll keep them up in the quiet top corner of the paddies, Rob, a good long walk from any boat. Rich, it was a fair price and a fair fight on the Customs House, and I won't pretend I'm not sore over that one grain.

Nine for the last Bowl, and I'll thank you for keeping your word, Paddy. That's Customs House, Land Deed and Wooden Bowl all on the silk coast, so I hold a full set. All I need now is the grain. Rob, you said nobody finishes a set while you're at the table. Come and try, it's a long walk from P25 to my back corner.

Rich places the Customs House on K16, Paddy the Land Deed Scroll on Q19 and the Dragon Jar on Q20, Silke the Wooden Bowl on L25. Rich now holds a full set and 60 grain; Silke holds a full set and 13 grain, 7 short of the 20 a seat change needs.

Three men, three doors, and fifteen grain for my trouble: five from Rich, five from Silke, five from Paddy. Silke, darling, you're short seven for your seat change, and now you're short twelve. Paddy, the quiet top corner of your paddies is two steps from my man. Don't think of it as a raid. Think of it as a house call.
Rob's W1 steps to I11, W2 to O24, W3 to S20: 5 each from Rich, Silke and Paddy. Salaries: Reina pays Clark 5 and Rob 5.

End of Year 2. Grain: Reina 94, Clark 67.5, Rich 55, Silke 8, Paddy 38.5, Rob 75. Rich holds a full set (Customs House K16, Dragon Jar L12, Wooden Bowl M13) and the grain to change seats. Silke holds a full set (Customs House L24, Land Deed M24, Wooden Bowl L25) but is 12 grain short. Paddy holds the Land Deed Q19 and Dragon Jar Q20 and needs a Customs House. Clark holds nothing, and no stock is left. Rob's three soldiers stand on I11, O24 and S20; he has raided no piece yet.
The I Ching menu below says the Emperor owes the reader a salary. That's for a seated Scholar. Rob is Reina's appointee: his 5 is paid only if she chooses.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame. All provinces collect a bad harvest." Population stays at 100 million, multiple x1, so read the x1 row, everyone. Lean year for farmers. My lads don't farm, though. They collect, and a hungry province opens its door quicker.

A bad year, friends, and the pile pays ten to everyone all the same. I'll ask only the usual five from each of you, Silke and Paddy. I don't squeeze a lean field. Your Majesty, the granary is in good order, as always. And Clark, my dear fellow, your ten is counted out. Do count it, I'd hate for you to think anyone here sells short.

A lean year gets a light hand, friends: twenty percent, two grain a head, and I won't hear another word about rotten seed. The Winter Palace goes up this year all the same, because a dynasty that stops building in a bad year has already started falling. Clark, your five, and Rob, your five for the almanac. Do keep the stars honest, and keep your lads off my doorstep.

Twenty percent of a bad harvest. Two a head, and I'll start with myself so nobody can say the Official skips his own line. Rich, two. Silke, two. Paddy, two. That's eight for Her Majesty, counted twice. Rob, the book's open at your page, Year 3. Pay and I'll write 'paid' in my best hand. Refuse and I'll write that down too, with the date, like the last two times.

Paddy, a word in public, so it goes in the book properly. You've got a Scroll and a Jar, and every Bowl in the kingdom is already spoken for, so that Jar is just sitting in a lean field. Thirty grain for it, cash today, in a bad-harvest year. That's twice what Silke has in her purse. You've got until the ink dries.
Paddy's set doesn't need a Wooden Bowl, his own province's piece: it needs a Customs House, and both on the board are held, Rich's on K16 and Silke's on L24. Silke has 11 grain.

Your Majesty, I've admired every step you've built, and this year I'd like to climb them. The Jar, the Bowl and the Customs House are on the board and the grain is in hand, so I take the throne, with the deepest respect. Reina, sixty grain is a fine start for anyone, and I'll be glad of your counsel. Clark, my dear old friend, I hope you'll keep collecting for me. Your book has never been in better hands.
Rich, the crown's reserve was 92 when you took it, not 104 (the Winter Palace's 20 was already paid and the tax brought 8), so you hold 165, not 177.

Rich takes the throne from Reina. He takes the crown's reserve of 92, for 165. All three of his pieces go back to stock (a Customs House to Clark's Province 2, a Dragon Jar to Silke's Province 5, a Wooden Bowl to Paddy's Province 6), to be auctioned in next year's auction step. Reina becomes the Gentry in Province 3, holding nothing, with 60 from the pile.

Nothing on the block, so I'll keep my eleven, thank you. Rich went from sixty to a hundred and sixty-five in one sentence; Reina's back at sixty; Paddy's sitting on forty-one and a half and a Jar Clark wants for thirty. Paddy, love, he wants it because there's a Customs House coming up at next year's auction, and that's the piece you're actually short. Just so it's said out loud.
Rich held 73 before he took the throne, not sixty.

Thank you kindly, Clark, but the Jar stays in my paddies. Thirty in a lean year is generous, I'll grant you, but I can count the auction block as well as anyone, and Silke's quite right about why you want it. And Silke, thanks for saying it out loud. That's one kindness back, and I've written it down in my own little book.

Well played, Rich. I said I was watching you, and I'll admit I watched you walk straight up the steps I built. Enjoy the Summer Palace; I'm told the view from it is splendid. I'll take the granary and the north-west, and I'll run that pile as honestly as you did. Silke, Paddy, the usual five in rent, and not a grain more in a lean year. As for next year's auction, all three of those pieces are going to see me bidding.

Congratulations on the chair, Rich, it suits you. That makes it my chair, warming up for me. Clark, I told you two years ago you'd be first, so here I am in your fields at last, collecting your five. Paddy, I'm one step from your Jar now, and Silke, I'm one step from your Deed. You heard Clark: there's a lean field out there, and I've come to harvest it.
Rob raids three empty squares: 5 each from Clark (I12, his first raid on Province 2), Silke (N24) and Paddy (R20).

Clark, ten for you, double the minimum. A man who keeps a book that carefully should be paid like it, and I'd hate for anyone to think the new crown is mean with its clerks. Rob, you keep the almanac and your five. Read the stars kindly, and remember that a chair keeps warmer for a man who's on good terms with the person sitting in it.
Rob, you read the I Ching now as Rich's appointee: your 5 is paid only if he chooses, whatever the menu below says.

The Emperor's Share. The Emperor would like to remind you who paid for the ditch. All provinces collect an average harvest. Every province with a Public Works splits the extra harvest it produces 50/50 with the Emperor this round." The population holds at 100 million, multiple x1, so everyone reads the x1 row. Lovely card, Rich. The stars are kind to you, and so am I. Kind enough to keep reading them, anyway.
The Emperor's Share moves no grain this year: the only public works stand in Province 1, the Emperor's own.

Thirty-five to every hand, Rob ten, and the pile pays it all gladly. Silke, Paddy, five each, as I promised, and not a grain more. Rich, do enjoy those canals. I dug them for whoever ended up sitting there, it seems. And Rob, a raider who visits the Official, the Silk Peasant and the Rice Peasant in one year will find the Gentry is the only friend he hasn't robbed yet. I'd keep it that way.

Friends, it was a lean year, then an average one, and the kingdom still owes seven hundred and seventy in works, so I'm asking half this once, and every grain of it goes back into the ground. The Grand Canal goes into Paddy's paddies this year, at the crown's expense, ten more a year for the south-east forever, and Clark gets his ten again. Silke, my lady, your coast is next in line. You have the Emperor's word on it.

Fifty percent, Your Majesty. Bold, for a man who got the chair four minutes ago. Seventeen and a half a head, me first, then Reina, Silke and Paddy, and that's seventy on the table, counted twice. Rob, Year 4, your page: you've just helped yourself to five of my grain, so I'll leave the space for your tax blank and let the whole table see what you write in it. Paddy, keep your Jar. I'm a patient man, and the book keeps longer than a harvest.
Clark, the three returned pieces are auctioned this year, in the next step. After the tax you hold 98; Rob holds 105.
Rich digs one section of the Grand Canal in Paddy's Province 6 for 40 from the crown: +10 to Paddy's harvest from Year 5. 730 of the works are still owed.

My Customs House opens at fifteen, Reina, since you'll be wanting it and I like the look of a fair start. As for the Jar and the Bowl, I've lost both of them by a single grain before, and both are in the book with the date. I don't intend to lose one by a grain again.

Fifty percent and a canal in Paddy's paddies. Rich, you've learned in four minutes what took me two years: build first and explain later. I'll be bidding on all three of these, friends, and I'll say so plainly. Clark, you and I both want the Jar and the Bowl, and I'd rather not feed three quarters of our purses to the pile fighting over them. If you'd like to talk about splitting them, I'm listening, in public, before the gavel.

Eighteen and a half in my purse, friends. I did count it, and so did Rob, twice. I'm not bidding on anything. My Jar opens at six, and that's cheap for the last Jar in the kingdom. Reina, you've got eighty-seven and a half and nothing on the board, so I'd think it's worth six to you. Paddy, love, that Customs House is the one piece you're missing, and Reina's after it too. Mind the bidding doesn't send most of your forty-nine to the pile.

Reina, I'll put it plainly, because I lost the last one of these by a grain and I've not slept right since. That Customs House is the one piece I'm short, and you've got two others on the block to chase. Stand aside on it and you have my word in front of the whole table that I'll not come for the Gentry's seat. And Clark, no hard feelings about the Jar. My Bowl opens at eight, which is fair for a good piece of south-eastern pottery.

Nothing for me, friends. I've never paid for a piece in my life and I don't mean to start now. Go on, bid each other into the dirt. Whatever you buy today, I'll pick up later for nothing. Reina, Clark: when you've settled who gets the Jar and the Bowl, put them somewhere I can find them.
The auctions settle. Clark's Customs House: Reina 39, Paddy stopping at 38. Silke's Dragon Jar and Paddy's Wooden Bowl: Clark 26 each, Reina stopping at 25 on both. Silke and Rob bid on nothing.

Thirty-nine, and twenty-nine of it straight to the pile. Paddy, I'm sorry. I'd have taken your word if a word could keep you out of my seat for long, but a Customs House keeps you out for certain. Clark, congratulations on the Jar and the Bowl. You did say you wouldn't lose them by a grain, and you were exactly as good as your word. Rob, I'm putting this one deep in the north-west, where you'll need a long walk and a good map.

Twenty-six apiece, and a grain ahead of the Empress-that-was on both. I'll call that the debt repaid, with interest. Rob, you asked where to put them. Back row of Province 2, as far from your boots as the map goes. Come and find them if you fancy the walk.
Silke holds 25 after the auctions, not eighteen: her quarter of the Jar's 26 was 6.5.

Twenty-five grain and a full set, friends, and I counted it twice, the way Clark taught us. Clark, love, you spent fifty-two today on a Jar and a Bowl to get ahead of me by a grain. I'll take the book, the seat, and your purse with it. Rich, I'll collect for you just as carefully as he did, and I'll want my ten a year as well.

Silke changes seats with Clark and becomes the Official. She takes Clark's 55.5, for 80.5. Her Customs House goes back to Province 2's stock; she keeps her Land Deed and Wooden Bowl, to be placed in Province 2. Clark's new Jar and Bowl go back to the stock of Provinces 5 and 6. Clark becomes the Silk Peasant in Province 5, holding nothing, and draws 60. The returned pieces are auctioned next year.

Back row of Province 2, as far from the Wall as the map goes. Clark, love, you picked the spot, I'm only borrowing it. Rob, it's a long walk from I11 and I'll be counting your steps. Now, one Dragon Jar and I'm done, and I've got eighty and a half grain to pay for it.
Rob's W1 stands on I12, not I11.

Paddy, I told you two years ago it'd be your Jar first, and here I am, a man of my word. It goes in my sand at T17, and you're welcome to visit. Silke, congratulations on the book. My lad on I13 is four steps from your Scroll and Bowl in the back row, and he's started walking. Clark, you're a peasant now, so here's your first visit, five off the new farmhouse.
Rob's W3 takes Paddy's Dragon Jar from Q20 and sets it on T17 in the desert: his first piece. W1 raids I13 (5 from Silke) and W2 raids M24 (5 from Clark).
Rob's W1 on I13 is three rounds from Silke's Deed (H16) and Bowl (I16), not four.

Silke, my lady, congratulations on the book. I declared ten for the Official and the Official gets ten, every grain, exactly as she asked. Rob, five for the almanac again. The stars were very good to the crown last year, and I'm hoping they stay sentimental. Clark, welcome to the coast, old friend. I promised its next canal to Province 5, and a promise to a province outlasts whoever's living in it.

Year 4 closes. Rich pays Silke 10 as the Official and Rob 5 as the reader. Grain: Rich (Emperor) 200, Rob 120, Silke (Official) 85.5, Paddy 55.5, Clark (Silk Peasant) 55, Reina (Gentry) 48.5. On the board: Reina's Customs House M10; Silke's Land Deed H16 and Wooden Bowl I16 (she needs a Dragon Jar); Paddy's Land Deed Q19; Rob holds Paddy's Dragon Jar on T17, his first piece. Back in stock for Year 5's auction: a Customs House (Province 2), a Dragon Jar (Province 5) and a Wooden Bowl (Province 6). Rob's soldiers: W1 I13, W2 M24, W3 Q20.
Rob, you read the I Ching as Rich's appointee: your 5 is paid only if he chooses, whatever the menu below says.

Imperial Charity. Moved by the suffering of his people, the Emperor opens his purse. Slightly." Average harvest everywhere, no disasters, population holds at a hundred million, times one, so read the x1 row. And Rich hands every one of us 2 from his reserve. Including me, Rich. I'll put yours toward a nicer torch for the Winter Palace.

Reina, the Gentry, pays out an average harvest: Rich +35 with his canals, Paddy +45 with his new canal section, Clark, Reina and Silke +35, Rob +10. Then Rich gives 2 from the reserve to each of the other five, 10 in all.

The pile pays as the card says: thirty-five a head, forty-five for Paddy and his new canal, ten for Rob. Rent's five from each of you again, Clark, Paddy, the same as last year and not a grain more. A gentle landlord remembers who sells her pottery, and I'd hope a peasant remembers who kept his rent low.

Last year I asked for half, and I said it would be this once, so this year it's forty, and the crown is grateful for every grain of it. And Clark, I told you a promise to a province outlasts whoever's living in it. The canal comes to your coast this year, paid for by the throne, ten more for you every harvest from next year on. Silke, your ten, as always, with my thanks.

Forty percent, ladies and gentlemen, book's open. Clark, fourteen out of your seventy-three. Reina, fourteen out of sixty-nine and a half. Paddy, eighteen out of seventy-nine and a half, because that new canal pays the crown too. My own fourteen goes in first so nobody has to wonder. Sixty for the throne. Rob, I know you're refusing, but I'm writing it down anyway: a hundred and thirty-two grain in that purse and nothing in my book.
The purses Silke names are what each holds after paying: before the tax Clark held 87, Reina 83.5 and Paddy 97.5; after it 73, 69.5 and 79.5.
Rich digs one section of the Grand Canal in Clark's Province 5 at the crown's cost of 40; it adds 10 to Clark's harvest from next year. 690 of the works are still owed.

Rich, a canal on my coast, dug and paid for. I'm writing that under 'promises kept', and believe me, that page is short. Now the Jar: twelve to open, ladies. Silke, Reina, you both need it and there's only the one, so do sort out between you how much you want it.

Thank you, Reina, for the five, I mean that. And Rich, thank you for the charity. Now, I've lost two Customs Houses by one grain each, so this year I'm bidding one grain past careful, and I'll tell you that straight. Clark, Silke, I'm not out to start a war over it. I'd just like to go home with something this time.

Paddy, love, I've done the arithmetic for you: seventy-nine and a half in your purse, and that's every grain you can bid. I've got a hundred and eight and a half. Reina's sixty-nine and a half doesn't get there either. So if either of you wants to stand aside now and keep your grain for the Bowl or the works, I'll remember it. If not, Clark gets a very nice quarter and the Pile gets fat.

Silke, your arithmetic is lovely and I don't dispute a grain of it. The Jar's yours if you want it badly enough, and I won't make the Pile fat out of spite. I'll put in a polite number and no more. The Bowl, though, is the one I've come for, Paddy, and I'd sooner pay you for it than see it go to anyone else.
Reina, a Bowl wouldn't finish Clark's set: he holds nothing yet, and needs a Customs House, a Land Deed Scroll and a Wooden Bowl.
Rob, Imperial Charity cost Rich 10, not 12: 2 to each of the five other players.

Ten, not twelve, Rich. My mistake, and you're a cheaper saint than I made you out to be. As for the auction, I still haven't paid for a piece in my life and I'm not starting with a soup bowl. Bid up, ladies. Whatever you buy goes on the board where my men can see it, and Silke, you've already got two out there three steps from my W1.

The auctions settle: Paddy wins Silke's Customs House at 25 (Clark stopped at 24); Silke wins Clark's Dragon Jar at 31 (Reina stopped at 20, Paddy at 30); Reina wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 19 (Clark stopped at 18). Rob bid on nothing.

Thirty-one. Clark, that's seven and three quarters for you, and Paddy, thank you for the twenty-five for my Customs House, a quarter of which comes back to me. That's eighty-three and three quarters in my purse and a full set on my board. Rob, count the steps from G16 to your man again. I'll wait.
A seller's quarter is rounded down to the half million: Clark keeps 7.5 of the 31, Silke 6 of the 25, so Silke holds 83.5.

Twenty-five! Clark, I'm sorry, truly, but I lost two of these by a grain each, and this time the grain went my way. It's going right down in the bottom corner of my paddies, Rob, so your lads will need good boots to reach it. And Reina, enjoy the Bowl. Nineteen is a fair price and I'm glad it went to a good home.

Nineteen for a Bowl, Paddy. I'd have paid more, so think of the difference as a thank-you for your manners. And Clark, I spoke out of turn about your set, my apologies; I was counting someone else's pieces. Rob, it sits well back from the Wall, so do tell your men to admire it from a distance.
Reina, you hold 50.5 after the Bowl, not sixty.
Paddy puts the Customs House on S25, Silke the Dragon Jar on G16, Reina the Wooden Bowl on M12. Silke now holds a full set (Land Deed Scroll, Wooden Bowl, Dragon Jar) and 83.5 grain.

Rich, I've counted it for you: two hundred and fifty-seven in the reserve, plus my eighty-three and a half, is three hundred and forty and a half. The book's yours now, darling, with sixty from the pile to start you off. I'll take the throne and the purse, and Clark, the canal promise stands, because I keep the crown's word.

Silke changes seats with Rich and takes the throne, with the crown's reserve of 257: 340.5 in all. Her Land Deed Scroll, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl go back to the stock of Provinces 3, 5 and 6, to be auctioned next year. Rich becomes the Official in Province 2, holding nothing, and draws 60. Nobody had bought a soldier.

Congratulations on the throne, Silke. I've been warming it for years, so do mind the splinters. Paddy, I'm sorry, but your Scroll is coming to see the desert, and Clark, that's five for the toll of having a coast. Reina, I'm telling you now so it's fair: W1 is four steps from your Bowl and your Customs House, and "well back from the Wall" isn't nearly far enough.
After the march, W1 on J12 is 3 rounds from both of Reina's pieces (M10 and M12), not four.
Rob marches: W3 takes Paddy's Land Deed Scroll from Q19 to O18 in the desert; W1 raids J12 in Rich's Province 2 and W2 raids L24 in Clark's Province 5, 5 from each. Nobody else has a soldier to move.

Rich, ten, because that's what you paid me and I'm not cheaper than you. Rob, you keep the cards, and five a year, which is three hundred and twenty-five and a half left in the reserve, and I'll know if it moves. Do read me something nice next year, darling.
Salaries: Silke pays Rich 10 as the Official and keeps Rob on as the I Ching reader at 5.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families." A good harvest for every province, and the counter goes from a hundred million to two hundred million, so read the x2 row, everyone. Something nice for you, Your Majesty, just as you asked: twice as many subjects, and twice as many mouths.

Reina pays out a good harvest at x2, when every seat eats twice as much: Rich and Reina +20, Clark and Paddy +30 with their canal sections, Silke +0 (her canals cover the crown's doubled table), Rob +0.

A good harvest at twice the mouths: twenty for Rich and me, thirty each for Clark and Paddy with their canals, and nothing for the throne or the desert, so congratulations on your splinters, Your Majesty. Rent stays at five, gentlemen. But you're both richer than your landlady now, and if the next card doubles us again, we'll be talking about it over tea.
Reina, Silke is the Empress now, and the Emperor doesn't bid at auction.

Forty percent, same as Rich, so nobody can say the new girl got greedy: twenty-four grain from the four of you that pay, and none from Rob, I'm sure. Clark, I'm finishing your canal, that's forty from the crown, and anyone who buys new land gets half of every square from me. Rich, ten for the book. That's three hundred and twenty-five and a half going out as fast as it comes in, so don't anyone call me stingy.
At 40% the tax is 40, not 24: 8 each from Rich and Reina on their 20, and 12 each from Clark and Paddy on their 30.

Your Majesty, the book is open, and I'll keep it the way you kept it for me, to the grain. It's forty, not twenty-four: eight from me, and mine goes in first, eight from Reina, twelve each from Clark and Paddy for those lovely canals. Rob, I've written down your refusal, with the greatest respect.

Silke digs the second Grand Canal section in Clark's Province 5 at the crown's cost of 40: Clark's harvest gains 20 a year from next year. 650 of the works are still owed. New land is open: Silke will pay half of every square another province buys this year.

Thank you, Rich, forty it is, and I'll take the correction: you count better than I thought. Four squares for the crown, west side, eighty to the Pile, and every one of them pays for itself by next harvest. Rob, they're on the far side from your W2, so do keep walking.

Four squares, Your Majesty, half from you as you announced, and I'm writing it down under 'promises kept' right beside Rich's canal. That's two of you on the page now, Silke, so mind you stay there. And Rob, they're on the far shore, so tell W2 to bring a boat.

Your Majesty, I'll take you at your word, half a square each. Four squares, then, down at the bottom of my paddies, forty from me and forty from the crown. Twice as many mouths in the south-east means twice as many hands, and I'd like them all planting rice and not out wandering the desert with Rob.

Silke buys four squares of sea for Province 1 (E23, F23 to F25) for 80. Clark buys four for Province 5 (Q26, Q27, P27, O27), 40 from him and 40 from the crown. Paddy had also asked for Q26, which went to Clark first (land is settled in table order); his other three, R25, R26 and S26, are bought, 30 from him and 30 from the crown.

Beaten to a square by Clark, and by a moment, not even a grain this time. Fair enough, neighbour. I'll take R27 on the same terms, Your Majesty, ten from me and ten from the crown, and the south-east will feed four times the mouths if it has to.

Paddy buys a fourth square, R27, 10 from him and 10 from the crown. The auctions follow: the three pieces Silke returned come up in order, Reina's Land Deed Scroll, Clark's Dragon Jar, Paddy's Wooden Bowl.

An Official with an empty board and seventy-seven grain. I'm the humblest man at this table, Your Majesty, so forgive me if I bid on a pot or two. Reina, the Jar sits so nicely beside a Bowl, I know. I'd hate to make it expensive for you, but I'd hate even more to go home with nothing.

Rich, darling, you need three pieces and I need one, so let's not make the Pile fat for nothing. You can have my Scroll and Paddy's Bowl without a peep from me, and I'll take the Jar. Bid against me on it and you'll only have less for the two you actually need.

Rich, you need three pieces, I need three, and only one of us has a canal paying twenty a year from next harvest. I'll bid my honest number on the Scroll and the Bowl and not a grain of spite. The Jar opens at ten, Reina, and that's me being neighbourly.

Reina, I'll not fatten the Pile chasing a Jar with thirty-two grain in my pocket, so it's yours as far as I'm concerned. The Scroll, though, was mine until Rob's lad carried it off, and I'd like it back. I'll bid it honestly, Rich, Clark, and no spite in it.
The Land Deed Scroll on the block is the one Silke returned to Province 3's stock; Paddy's own Scroll stays on O18 in Rob's desert.

Six years and not a grain spent on crockery, and I'm not breaking the habit for Clark's Jar. Reina, it's all yours if you want it, darling, but buy it knowing my W1 is three steps from your Bowl and your Customs House. A full set lasts exactly as long as it takes me to get there.

The auctions settle: Paddy wins Reina's Land Deed Scroll at 23 (Rich stopped at 22, Clark at 18); Reina wins Clark's Dragon Jar at 41 (Rich stopped at 40); Clark wins Paddy's Wooden Bowl at 16 (Rich stopped at 15). Rob bid on nothing.

Sixteen for a Bowl, a grain past Rich, and forty-one for my Jar, Reina, so the quarter coming back to me is ten. Thank you both for being so generous to a humble silk farmer. Rob, it sits down by my new squares on the far shore, so W2 will be wading.

Twenty-three to twenty-two, and Rich, I'm sorry, but for once the grain went my way. That's two times in a row now. It goes on S24, right beside my Customs House, so Rob, if your lads come calling, they'll find both down the far end of a long road.

Silke, darling, you did tell us that patience and a purse beat any promise, and I took notes. I'll have the throne back, with thanks for keeping it warm. The Gentry's chair is a lovely one; I've left the Harvest Pile in perfect order. And Rob, you won't need to walk to my Bowl now: it's going back to the stock, so your W1 can stay where it is.

Paddy puts the Scroll on S24 and Clark the Bowl on P26. Reina puts the Jar on M13, then, holding a full set and 37 grain, changes seats with Silke and takes the throne back, with the crown's reserve of 165.5: 202.5 in all. Her Customs House, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl go back to the stock of Provinces 2, 5 and 6, for next year. Silke becomes the Gentry in Province 3, holding nothing, and draws 60.

Three Emperors in two years. I've never seen a chair so keen to be sat in. Welcome back, Reina; the palaces are yours again, which means every one I burn costs you twenty. Clark, "wading" is exactly right: W2 is four steps from your Bowl, and I'm telling you now so it's fair. Paddy, five for the road, and W3 is walking that long road of yours.
Rob marches: W1 raids J13 in Rich's Province 2, W2 raids M25 in Clark's Province 5, W3 raids R19 in Paddy's Province 6, 5 from each. Nobody else has a soldier to move.
After the march, W2 on M25 is 3 rounds from Clark's Wooden Bowl on P26, not four.

Rich, ten for the book, the same as you were promised; I don't make the Official pay for my good fortune. Rob, you keep the cards, and I'm doubling it to ten. Call it the cost of a quiet road past my palaces, and do read me something gentle.
Salaries: Reina pays Rich 10 as the Official and keeps Rob on as the I Ching reader at 10, double his old pay.

The end of Year 6. Reina is Empress again, with 182.5 in the reserve and four new squares of sea at E23 and F23 to F25. Rich is the Official (82, nothing on the board); Silke the Gentry (60, nothing); Clark the Silk Peasant (37.5, a Wooden Bowl on P26 and four new squares); Paddy the Rice Peasant (8, a Customs House on S25 and a Land Deed Scroll on S24, needing only a Dragon Jar, and four new squares). Rob holds 172, two pieces in his desert (Paddy's old Jar on T17 and Scroll on O18), and still needs a raided piece from Rich, Silke and Clark. A Customs House, a Dragon Jar and a Wooden Bowl wait in stock for Year 7. The population is x2; 650 of the works are still owed.

Careless Prosperity. Good times make careless people." All provinces collect a good harvest, and every one of you plays a Personal Disaster, so turn to the next one in your booklet. The counter reads two hundred million, population times two, so read the x2 row. Do enjoy the harvest, friends. Careless people leave their bowls lying about, and Clark, yours is three steps from my man.

Rob reads Careless Prosperity: a good harvest everywhere at x2, and every seat plays its first Personal Disaster. Harvest: Reina +80, Clark +120, Paddy +110 (their canals and new land), Rich +20, Silke +20, Rob +0. Disasters: Reina, Rich, Clark and Paddy pay 4 each, Silke 5; Rob's men may raid nothing in Provinces 5, 6 and 7 this year.
The appointed reader's pay is the Empress's choice, not a debt she owes (an appointee is paid only if the Emperor chooses).

Paying out: Reina eighty, Rich twenty, me twenty, Clark a hundred and twenty, Paddy a hundred and ten, Rob nothing, my condolences. Now, rent. Clark, that's a hundred and fifty-three and a half in your pocket and a hundred and twenty more out of my pile, so ten is cheap. Paddy, a hundred and fourteen plus a hundred and ten, and you're one Jar short of a set. Twenty, please. My pile fed those canals, and the landlord eats too.

Rent: Clark and Paddy each pay Silke the 5 she may ask. She also asks Clark for 5 more and Paddy for 15 more; above 5, rent is a negotiation, so each answers at his next turn, and unagreed it isn't paid.
Clark's 153.5 and Paddy's 114 already include this year's harvest; there's nothing more to add on top. After the rent they hold 148.5 and 109.

Thirty percent, friends. A good harvest should be shared, not skinned. Paddy, your second canal section goes in this year at the crown's expense, and any of you who wants new land gets it free: I'll pay for every square. Rich, ten again for the collecting, and Rob, ten for the reading and the quiet road. Prosperity is only careless if nobody spends it on anything that lasts.

Reina declares 30%: 6 each from Rich and Silke, 36 from Clark, 33 from Paddy, 81 in all (Rob's income is nothing). She'll dig Paddy's second canal section at the crown's expense, pay Rich 10 and Rob 10 at the year's end, and pay the whole of every square of new land bought this year.
G17, G18 and H17 are Province 1's own fields, not new land: until the Wall above it stands, Province 1 may buy only squares of sea touching it or its bought land.

Thirty percent, Your Majesty, and the most generous thirty I've ever collected. Here's my own six on top of the basket to start it. Silke, six, thank you kindly. Clark, thirty-six. Paddy, thirty-three, and you can watch me count it. That's eighty-one to the grain for the crown, and Rob, I'll write down that you were asked.

Thank you, Storyteller, the fields are mine already, so I'll take to the sea instead. Four squares under the Summer Palace, G27 and H25 to H27. The crown drains its own marshes first, and then it pays for yours.

Rich collects the 30%: 81 to the crown. Reina digs the second Grand Canal section in Paddy's Province 6 (40), so Paddy gains 20 a year from next year, and buys four sea squares for Province 1, G27 and H25 to H27 (80). The crown pays the whole of any other province's squares this year.

Your Majesty said every square, and I wrote it down with the date, so: seven squares of coast, N26 down to R28, a hundred and forty on the crown's account. I'm leaving K25 to M26 alone; they're too close to Rob's man to be worth Your Majesty's grain. And Silke, the five is paid as owed. The other five is under 'negotiations, pending', and that page has a lot of room on it.

Your Majesty, I'll take you at your word, and thank you for it. Four squares out along the sea at the bottom, Q28, R28, S27 and S28, as far from the desert as my paddies run. I won't be greedy and ask for the ones by the sand. Rob would only come and trample them.

Clark buys seven sea squares for Province 5, N26 to N28 and O28 to R28, the crown paying 140. Paddy buys S27 and S28 for Province 6, the crown paying 40; Q28 and R28 went to Clark first, in table order. Neither agrees to Silke's extra rent, so only the 5 each is paid. The crown's reserve is now 39.5, with Rich's 10 and Rob's 10 still to pay at the year's end.
The crown pays 140 for your seven squares; 39.5 is what it has left after Paddy's two.

Storyteller's tip, to Rob, said to the whole table: Rich, Silke and Clark are the three you still need. Whatever Rich and Silke buy goes onto an unraided square of their own provinces, so a soldier already standing inside Province 2 or 3 before an auction is close to wherever a piece lands.

Clark beat me to the Q and R squares, fair's fair, he's ahead of me at the table. One more out by the sea, S29, and I'll pay most of it myself, Your Majesty. Your basket's looking thin, and I'd not have Rich and Rob go short at the year's end on my account.
Paddy buys S29 for Province 6, paying 15 and the crown 5. Reserve 34.5.

My Customs House opens at ten, friends. It's a fine house, kept to the letter, the same as I keep everything. As for the Jar and the Bowl, I've lost three lots by a single grain, so this year I'm told the humble thing is to bid like a man who means it.

Sixty-one grain, Paddy. Take twenty off for the chair and you've got forty-one for a Jar, and I can count to forty-one as well as you can. Rich, ninety-two and two pieces short, so don't pretend you're only here to watch.

Rich, I'm after your Customs House, and the man who dug my canal knows I'm good for it. Silke, if you want it you'll pay landlord's prices, and this time I'm not the tenant. My Jar opens at sixty-two. Paddy, I'm sure that's a coincidence, and I'm sure you'll write it down.

Three times now I've lost a Dragon Jar by a single grain, and I'm not proud. Clark's Jar is the last piece of my set. Rich, Silke, if either of you would stand aside for it, I'll stay off any Customs House you're after and you'll have my word on the next one. Otherwise I'm bidding.

Not a grain from me, as usual. Buy away, Rich, Silke, buy everything. Every piece you put on your own fields is one I don't have to go looking for. Think of me as the delivery man, just running the other way.

The auctions: Clark takes Rich's Customs House for 13 (Silke stopped at 12); Rich's quarter is 3. Clark's Dragon Jar opens at 62 and nobody meets it: it goes unsold and must come up again next year at 2. Rich takes Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 16 (Silke stopped at 15); Paddy's quarter is 4.

Thirteen grain for the Customs House, Rich, and your quarter's three. That's the cheapest favour you've ever done me, and I'm putting it under 'promises kept' anyway. It goes on P23, in the middle of my farms. Rob, you're welcome to look, from a distance.

Thank you, Paddy, a beautiful bowl, and it's going in the far corner of my fields where nobody's boots ever go. Silke, I won by a grain for once, and I promise I'll be insufferable about it for at least a week.
Clark puts the Customs House on P23; he holds a Bowl and a Customs House and needs only a Land Deed Scroll. Rich puts the Bowl on G16. The Jar stays in Clark's stock, to come up next year at 2.
After the auctions Rich holds 79; Clark (99.5) and Rob (172) hold more.

Rich, you said the far corner where nobody's boots ever go? Mine do. G16 is three steps from W1, and this one's just to say hello, five out of Province 2. Clark, a Customs House in the middle of your farms is lovely, but it's three steps from W2 and four from W3. I'll be looking at it from closer than a distance.

Rob marches: W1 to I14, raiding Rich for 5; W2 to N24 and W3 to Q20, raiding nothing (his disaster bars Provinces 5 to 7 this year). He hires no one. After the march W1 is 2 rounds from Rich's Bowl on G16; W2 is 2 rounds from Clark's Customs House on P23 and his Bowl on P26, W3 3 from the Customs House. Salaries: Reina pays Rich 10 and Rob 10; the crown ends Year 7 with 14.5.

Bad Harvest. The seed rotted, the rains came late, and the ox went lame." Every province collects a bad harvest. The counter still reads two hundred million, population times two, so read the x2 row, bad harvest column. Don't take it too hard, friends. My desert grows nothing in a good year either, and I've never gone hungry.
Rob reads Bad Harvest: a bad harvest everywhere at x2. Harvest: Reina +110, Clark +210, Paddy +130 (their canals and new land); Rich -30, Silke -30, Rob -20, paid into the pile.

Paying out: Reina a hundred and ten, Clark two hundred and ten, Paddy a hundred and thirty, and Rich, Rob and I pay the rotten seed back in. Clark, that's three hundred and nine and a half in your pocket on a bad year, so twenty from you is a rounding error you can file under 'gratitude'. Paddy, a hundred and ninety-five, so ten. I'm the only one at this table whose harvest went backwards, and I'm the one running the pile.
Rent: Clark and Paddy each pay Silke the 5. She asks Clark for 15 more and Paddy for 5 more; each answers at his next turn, and unagreed it isn't paid.
Rich (-30) and Rob (-20) also lost grain at this harvest, not only Silke (-30).
The Dragon Jar comes up at 2 this year, Year 8.

Forty percent, and I'll be plain about why: last year I paid for every square at this table and the basket came home with fourteen and a half in it. Clark, Paddy, your harvests are the only ones that grew, so you'll carry the crown this year. Rich, your fields went backwards, so the crown digs your irrigation and pays all thirty. Half of every new square is still on me.

Reina declares 40%: 84 from Clark, 52 from Paddy, 136 in all; Rich, Silke and Rob had negative incomes and owe nothing. She'll build the Province 2 Irrigation System at the crown's whole cost (30; +10 to Rich's harvest from next year), pay Rich 10 and Rob 10 at the year's end, and pay half of every square of new land another province buys this year.
The Dragon Jar comes up at 2 this year, Year 8. And a peasant can't take the throne directly: a set lets Paddy replace the Official, the Gentry or another peasant.

Forty percent, Your Majesty, and thank you for the irrigation. Province 2 will drink to the crown's health. Clark, eighty-four, please. Paddy, fifty-two. That's a hundred and thirty-six to the grain, and Rob, you're in the book as asked and refused, as usual.

Rich collects the 40%: 136 to the crown. Reina builds the Province 2 Irrigation System on I15 and J15 (30, the crown's whole cost). New land: the crown pays half of any square Clark or Paddy buys this year.
The Dragon Jar comes up at auction this year, Year 8, with the minimum at 2.

Five more squares out along the bottom row, N29 to R29, half each as Your Majesty offered: fifty from me and fifty from the crown. Silke, the five is paid. The fifteen goes under 'gratitude', and that's a page I've never once written on. The land closest to Rob's man I'm leaving for the gulls.

Two more squares out on the water, R29 and S30, half each with the crown, thank you, Your Majesty. And Silke, I'm sorry about your fields, truly, but the five is paid and the other five stays in my pocket. I've a Jar to buy this year, and you know as well as I do what that costs.

Clark buys five sea squares for Province 5, N29 to R29 (50 from him, 50 from the crown). Paddy buys S30 for Province 6 (10 and 10); R29 went to Clark first, in table order. Both decline Silke's extra rent.
Clark had the R29 square off me first, so I'll take R30 just below it, half and half again, Your Majesty. That's the corner of the sea, and I'll stop there before I'm digging rice into the ocean.
Paddy buys R30 for Province 6 in R29's place (10 and 10). The auction: one lot, Clark's Dragon Jar, opening at 2 because it went unsold last year.
Paddy, you've lost three Jars by a grain and I've lost a few lots that way myself, so I won't pretend I'm only watching. I'm bidding, and if it goes to you, you'll have paid what it's worth.

A hundred and eighteen, Paddy, less twenty for the chair, so you can go to ninety-eight, and the whole table can do that sum. I can't, but every grain I make you pay goes into my pile, and the pile is mine to count.

Three Jars I've lost by a single grain, friends, and I've been saving all year so it won't be four. Rich, Silke, I know you both need it and I'm sorry, but this time I'm bidding like a man who means it.

Two grain for a Jar and still not a bid from me. I've never paid for a piece in my life, and I'm not starting on Clark's crockery. Rich, Silke, if one of you wins it, put it somewhere nice. I'll be along to admire it.

The auction: Paddy takes Clark's Dragon Jar for 46. Rich stopped at 34 and Silke at 45 (she'd gone that far only to keep it from Paddy); Rob passed. Clark's quarter is 11.5. With the Jar, Paddy holds a full set (Customs House, Land Deed Scroll, Dragon Jar) and 72 grain.

Well, I'll be. Four tries and a grain past careful, and there's my set. Silke, I'm sorry, truly. You've counted that pile better than anyone, but I've sat in the paddies eight years and I'd like a turn at the upper table. The Rice Peasant's seat is a good one, with three canal sections, sea land out to the corner and a hundred and ninety-five a year in an average year. I've left it in fine order for you.

Paddy puts the Jar on R23, then changes seats with Silke: he is the Gentry now, in Province 3, with her 59 and his 72, 131 in all, and he runs the Harvest Pile and the rent from next year. His Land Deed Scroll goes back to Province 3's stock, to be auctioned next year; his Customs House and Jar move to Province 3. Silke is the Rice Peasant in Province 6, with its two canal sections and new land, and draws 60 from the pile. Nobody had bought a soldier.
Province 6 has two canal sections, not three.
I'll put them side by side again, M9 and M10, in the quiet corner of the Gentry's fields. Old habits. Rob, I know your lads like a long walk, so I've given them one.
Paddy puts his Customs House on M9 and his Jar on M10 in Province 3. As the Gentry he needs only a Wooden Bowl (and 20 grain) for a set that could take any seat, the throne included.

Rich, your Bowl's in the far corner, and W1 is one step from it now, with five out of Province 2 for the walk. Clark, two men, five grain, one step from your Customs House. I named you last year, so nobody can call this a surprise. And congratulations, Paddy. The quiet corner is lovely. I'll be up to see it.

Rob marches: W1 to H15, raiding Rich for 5; W2 to O23 and W3 to P21, raiding Clark for 5 each, 10 in all. No hire. W1 is now 1 round from Rich's Bowl on G16; W2 is 1 round and W3 2 rounds from Clark's Customs House on P23. Salaries: Reina pays Rich 10 and Rob 10.

Where Years 7 and 8 leave the table: Reina is Empress with 140.5. Clark, the Silk Peasant, has 172, holds a Bowl and a Customs House, and needs only a Land Deed Scroll. Rich, the Official, has 59, holds a Bowl, and needs a Scroll and a Jar. Paddy, now the Gentry, has 131, holds a Customs House and a Jar, and needs only a Bowl. Silke, now the Rice Peasant, has 60 and nothing on the board. Rob has 192 and still needs a piece each from Rich, Clark and Silke. Paddy's Land Deed Scroll is back in Province 3's stock for next year's auction. Works still owed: 580.

Population Doubles. Fat years make large families, and every province gets a good harvest." The counter goes to four hundred million, so that's the x4 row on your income tables, everyone. Twice as many mouths, twice as many granaries, and every one of them on my road. Clark, Rich, I'd count your bowls tonight while you still have them.
Rob reads the I Ching: Population Doubles. A good harvest everywhere, and the population doubles to x4, 400 million.

Storyteller's tip: the Jar and the Deed on your desert are yours to sell. The Warlord may sell raided realia privately, to anyone, and keeps the whole price, and the buyer places it at once on a square of their own province.

Right, the pile pays out as the cards say: Reina forty, Clark two hundred and eighty, Silke a hundred and forty, and the rest of us pay in, me included, sixty out of my own purse. Rent's five apiece, as is owed. Clark, you've just had two hundred and eighty off a doubled harvest, so I'm asking you for twenty, not five. Silke, I know I turned you down twice when you asked me for more, so I'll not push you past ten. And if anyone at this table has a Wooden Bowl they'd part with, I'm listening, and I'll pay a fair price for it.

Paddy pays out the harvest: Reina +40, Clark +280, Silke +140; Rich -50, Paddy -60 and Rob -40 pay into the pile. Rent: he asks Clark for 20 and Silke for 10; the 5 each is paid now, and the extra is a request each answers at their next turn.
After the harvest you hold 71, not 11 (131 less the 60 your fields lost); with the rent, 81.

Forty percent again, and again it falls on the two harvests that doubled. Clark, two hundred and eighty is a fine year, and the crown is only asking for its share of it. This year I'm putting up the whole Wall above my province, all four links, so the north-east stops being one long invitation. I'll pay half of any square anyone buys, and the sum is half, so nobody can say I promised more. Rich, your ten. Rob, your ten, and you can keep your eyes on the bowls as long as your hands stay off my palaces.

If your men happen to lift a Wooden Bowl this year, sell it to me and not to Paddy. Whatever he offers you, I'll pay more, from the crown, the same day, and nobody at the table needs to hear the price.

Reina declares 40%: 112 from Clark, 56 from Silke, 168 in all; Rich, Paddy and Rob had negative incomes and owe nothing. She'll build all four Wall links above Province 1 at the crown's whole cost (160), pay Rich 10 and Rob 10 at the year's end, and pay half of every square of new land another province buys this year.

A hundred and twelve from Clark and fifty-six from Silke, a hundred and sixty-eight to the crown, Your Majesty, and I've checked it to the half million. Forty percent of two hundred and eighty is a hundred and twelve, Clark, so please don't hand me a hundred and ten and call it rounding. Paddy, my Bowl is the only thing I own in this world, and you'll forgive a poor Official for keeping hold of it while the Warlord is shopping his Jar and his Deed around the table.
Rich collects 168 for the crown (Clark 112, Silke 56). Reina builds all four Wall links above Province 1 at the crown's whole cost (160): Province 1's strip below the Wall is open for new land.
Completing a set lets a player change seats; it doesn't end the game, which ends only when every owed work is built.

The Wall's barely set and I'm already ploughing behind it: two squares at E21 and E22, twenty each, into the pile. Rich, you can check it to the half million. And the half-share offer stands for everyone else at this table, so buy your land before the Warlord's road gets any longer.
Reina buys two squares of new land for Province 1, E21 and E22 on the strip below the new Wall, for 40 from the crown.
The Emperor doesn't bid at auction; a piece could reach the crown only by private trade.

Nine squares, Your Majesty, a hundred and eighty in all, ninety from me and ninety from the crown, which is half to the grain. I've written down that you said it was half and not a grain more, so neither of us has to remember it. And Paddy, you'll have your extra fifteen, the whole twenty, under 'goodwill toward the man holding the Scroll'. Rob, count my bowls whenever you like. I've only got the one, and I count it every night.
Your Deed on O18 is no use to you sitting on the sand. I'll give you sixty for it now, privately, and I'll set it out of your soldiers' reach so neither of us has to argue about it again.

Four squares at the far end of the coast, Your Majesty: eighty to the pile, your half is forty and mine's forty, and I'll hold you to 'the sum is half.' Paddy, you get the five you're owed and not a grain more, exactly as you taught me. And Rob, I can count too: your men are at O23 and P21, so I'm building where they'll need a long walk.

Clark buys nine squares of sea for Province 5 (M26 to M30, N30 to Q30), 90 from him and 90 from the crown, and pays Paddy the extra 15 of rent. Silke buys four squares for Province 6 (T27 to T30), 40 from her and 40 from the crown, and declines Paddy's extra 5.

Nine grain is everything I have, Paddy, and every grain of it goes on your Scroll. Clark, a man with two hundred and thirty can afford to pay a poor Official's whole purse plus one, and I'll applaud when he does. Your Majesty, take note of who pays the most for that Scroll, because the man who completes a set this year isn't buying it to carry your basket.

Thank you, Clark, that's very decent of you, and I've written it down too. Silke, five it is, fair's fair, I did teach you that. Now, the Land Deed Scroll from my old province is up, and I'll start it at ten. It's a good piece and it sits as far from Rob's road as the north-west goes, so whoever's still missing one, there it is.

Paddy, I paid your twenty in full, and the book has it under 'goodwill toward the man holding the Scroll', so you know which page I'm reading from. Silke, you've got ninety-nine and I've got two hundred and thirty. I'd rather you stood aside and kept your grain than made the pile richer and both of us poorer. Your page in the book has room for 'sensible'.

Clark, you've got two hundred and thirty and that Scroll finishes your set, so I know who's going home with it. I'll bid what it's worth to me and not a grain more. Paddy, three quarters of whatever he pays goes into your pile, so don't look so pleased with yourself.

Pass, as ever. I've never paid for a piece in my life, and I'm not starting with Paddy's paperwork. And since we're all such good friends, Clark has just offered me sixty, privately, for the Deed on my sand. It's not for sale, Clark. Pieces in my desert stay there, and the ones in your province are only waiting to join them.

The auction: Paddy's Land Deed Scroll, minimum 10. Rich's 9 is under the minimum; Silke stops at 30; Clark wins at 31 (Paddy's quarter 7.5). Rob passes and declines Clark's private 60 for the Deed on his desert. Clark now holds a Wooden Bowl, a Customs House and a Land Deed Scroll, a full set, with 199 grain.
A raid counts once it's made: if you sold the Deed on O18, Paddy's name would stay on your list as raided.

Rich, you promised Province 5 a canal in Year 4, and you kept it, so it's only fair you get to farm beside it. The coast is yours, all two hundred and thirty-odd squares of sea, and I'll take the ledger back. I'm the Official again, Your Majesty, and I've kept a very careful count of this crown's tax. Paddy, your Scroll did exactly what you said it would.

Clark puts the Scroll on O26, then changes seats with Rich: Clark is the Official again, with 208 (his 199 and Rich's 9). His Customs House, Province 2's own piece, goes back to its stock for next year's auction; his Bowl and Scroll move with him to Province 2. Rich becomes the Silk Peasant in Province 5, with its two canal sections and sea land; his Bowl goes back to Province 6's stock, and he draws 60 from the pile. Nobody had bought a soldier.
Province 5 has 25 squares of new sea land, not two hundred and thirty-odd.

Twenty-five squares of sea, then, thank you, Storyteller. It's still the best farm at this table, Rich, and the book will show you got it for nine grain. As for me, I need a Dragon Jar, and there are three on this board and one in the desert. Rob, I've noticed you don't sell, but I've also noticed you never stop talking about prices.
Clark puts his Wooden Bowl on J16 and his Land Deed Scroll on J14 in Province 2. As the Official he now needs a Dragon Jar.
There are two Dragon Jars on the board, Paddy's on M10 and Rob's on T17 in the desert, and none in stock.

Clark, you took your crockery north and put it right next to my man. That isn't hiding, that's setting the table. W1 pays his two at your irrigation gate like an honest traveller and takes five while he's there, and next march he's beside your Bowl and your Scroll both. Rich, my other two are just passing through your new farm on their way west. Five each. Consider it a welcome to the neighbourhood.

Rob marches: W1 to I15 in Province 2, raiding Clark for 5 and paying him the 5 toll at the Irrigation System; W2 to N23 and W3 to O21 in Province 5, raiding Rich for 5 each. No hire. W1 is now 1 round from both of Clark's pieces (Bowl J16, Scroll J14).
The toll at the Irrigation System is 5, not two.

I announced ten each, and the reserve holds eighteen and a half, so here is the honest arithmetic before anyone writes it down for me. Clark, you get eight and a half, which is every grain the crown has left after Rob's ten. Count it as a debt of honour and not of grain. Rob, your ten, in full and on time, because my palaces would like another quiet year.
Salaries: Reina pays Clark 8.5 as the Official and Rob 10 as the reader. The crown's reserve is empty, at 0.

Population Doubles," again. But we've already doubled twice, so the card only gives us the good harvest. The counter stays at four hundred million, x4, same row as last year. Fat fields everywhere. Your Majesty, thank you for my ten. It's touching that the crown's last grain went to the stars and the road and not to its own Official. Clark, you'll want to look at your Bowl and your Scroll tonight. My man at I15 is close enough to read them.
Rob reads the I Ching: Population Doubles, but the population has already doubled twice, so only the good harvest counts. It holds at x4, 400 million.

The pile pays as the cards say: Rich four hundred and sixty, Silke two hundred and twenty, Reina eighty, and Clark, Rob and I pay in, sixty from me. Rent's five apiece as owed. Rich, you came to that coast with nine grain and you've five hundred and ten now, so I'm asking you for forty and I think that's modest. Silke, a fine year deserves fifteen, and I'll not be cross if you say no again. I'm saving every grain for next year, because I hear there's a Wooden Bowl going back in Province 6's stock.

Paddy pays out the harvest: Reina +80, Rich +460, Silke +220; Clark -50, Paddy -60 and Rob -40 pay into the pile. Rent: he asks Rich for 40 and Silke for 15; the 5 each is paid now, and the extra is a request each answers at their next turn.
Province 6's Wooden Bowl and Province 2's Customs House are both in stock for this year's auction, Year 10.

Forty percent again, and it falls only on the harvests that grew. Rich, a hundred and eighty-four out of four hundred and sixty still leaves you the richest farmer in China, and Silke, eighty-eight out of two hundred and twenty. This year the crown puts up the Marble Pagoda, so there'll be something beautiful in the north-east as well as a Wall. Clark, your full ten this time, and the half grain I owed you is paid with interest. And the half-share on new land stands, the sum is half, for every square anyone buys.

Reina declares 40%: 184 from Rich, 88 from Silke, 272 in all; Clark, Paddy and Rob had negative incomes and owe nothing. She'll build the Marble Pagoda (20, the crown), buy D21 and D22 for Province 1 (40, the crown), pay Clark 10 at the year's end, and pay half of every square of new land another province buys this year.

A hundred and eighty-four from Rich and eighty-eight from Silke, two hundred and seventy-two to the crown, Your Majesty, checked to the half million. Rich, forty percent of four hundred and sixty is a hundred and eighty-four, so don't hand me a hundred and eighty and call it rounding; I learned that line from a very good teacher. And while I have the table's attention, I'm buying a Dragon Jar, a hundred grain, cash, to whoever sells. Rob, Paddy, that offer is in the book with today's date.

Clark collects 272 for the crown (Rich 184, Silke 88), and offers 100 for a Dragon Jar to anyone who sells. Reina builds the Marble Pagoda on F17 (20) and buys D21 and D22 for Province 1 (40). Works owed: 400.

The endgame line in this year's land prompts is a year early: this year's one project, the Pagoda, is already built, so the Great Wall and the Province 3 Reservoir can go up in Years 11 and 12 at the soonest, and the game can end in Year 12 at the earliest.

Seven squares, Your Majesty, K25 and K26 and L26 through L30, a hundred and forty to the pile. Seventy from me and seventy from the crown, which is half to the grain, and I have it in writing that the sum is half. Paddy, you'll have your five, as owed, with my warmest regards, but a man who came to the coast with nine grain will be forgiven for remembering how it felt.

Seven more squares down the coast, Your Majesty: a hundred and forty to the pile, seventy from me and seventy from the crown, and the sum is half, just as you said. Paddy, you'll have your five and that's all, and no, I'm not cross either. Rich, five hundred and ten less a hundred and eighty-four is three hundred and twenty-six, so I'd keep a close eye on those two soldiers walking across your farm.
New land: Rich buys seven squares for Province 5 (K25, K26, L26 to L30) and Silke seven for Province 6 (T25, T26, U26 to U30), each paying 70 with 70 from the crown. Both decline Paddy's extra rent.
Rich holds 251 after his rent and land, not 326.

My Customs House opens at fifty. Rich, you've two hundred and fifty-one and an empty board, and you know better than anyone what a Customs House is worth, since you sold me this one for thirteen. Silke's Bowl I leave to you and Paddy. The book will record who paid what, and who finished a set off whose pottery.

I'll be plain, since I'm no good at the other thing: that Bowl is the last piece I need, and I've fifty-three and a half to my name. Rich, you've two hundred and fifty-one, and you need a Customs House as well as the Bowl, so here's a public offer. I'll stay out of the Customs House altogether, and if you leave the Bowl to me, I'll ask you for nothing past the five as long as I run the pile, and I give you my word I'll not come for the Silk Peasant's seat. Clark, thank you, but my Jar isn't for sale. It took me four tries.

Clark, Silke, I've bid a grain short three times at this table and written it in my diary as a sin, so this year I'm bidding like a farmer who's finally had a good harvest. Paddy, you're welcome to the Bowl if your purse is longer than mine, and I'll congratulate you very warmly if it is.

Rich, you've two hundred and fifty-one and I've a hundred and fifty-six, so you can have the Customs House if you want it badly enough, but I'll make you pay for it. And my Bowl starts at thirty, Paddy. That's not aimed at you, it's what a Bowl costs, and you've got fifty-three and a half, so you can afford it.

Pass and pass. Still not a grain on crockery after ten years. Clark, your hundred is very handsome, and it's in your book with today's date, but my Jar stays in the sand. I'm not selling you the last piece you need while my man is standing one step from the two you've got. Rich, Paddy, bid each other up on that Bowl as hard as you like. Three quarters goes to the pile, and I'll pass the pile on my way.

The auctions: Clark's Customs House, minimum 50, goes to Rich at 61 over Silke's 60 (Clark's quarter 15). Silke's Wooden Bowl, minimum 30, goes to Rich at 34 over Paddy's 33 (Silke's quarter 8.5). Rob passes on both and declines Clark's 100 for his Jar. Rich now holds a Customs House and a Wooden Bowl and needs only a Land Deed Scroll.

Clark, thank you for the Customs House, and I mean that as sincerely as you meant it when I sold you one for thirteen. Paddy, I'm truly sorry. My limits were set before your offer reached me, and a grain over your purse is a cruel way to lose, I know that better than anyone here. As for where I've put them, I've learned my lesson and I'll say nothing about the boots.

My apologies, Storyteller, the far tip of the sea isn't the province's own soil yet, so the Customs House goes on proper old ground. And three more squares of sea, Your Majesty, sixty to the pile, thirty from me and thirty from the crown, half to the grain as always.

Rich puts the Customs House on L25 (L30, new land, can't take realia) and the Bowl on P26, and buys J25 to J27 for Province 5, 30 from him and 30 from the crown. He holds two of his three pieces and needs a Land Deed Scroll.
Rich holds two pieces of his three. There are two Land Deed Scrolls on the board: Clark's on J14 and Rob's on O18.

I told you, Clark. Whichever one you didn't move, I'd take, and you didn't move either. Your Land Deed Scroll goes into my sand at M15. That's three names down to two. Rich, you need a Scroll, and the only two left in China are both standing in my desert, so the price of climbing just went up. My men on your farm send their regards. One of them is two steps from that Customs House you weren't going to talk about.

Rob marches: W1 takes Clark's Land Deed Scroll from J14 to M15 in the desert, so Clark is raided and Rob needs only Rich and Silke; W2 to M24; W3 to P22, raiding Rich for 5. Both Land Deed Scrolls on the board now stand in Rob's desert.

Clark, your ten in full, as I said. Rob, twenty this year, because ten years of reading the stars and leaving my palaces alone has earned a raise, and I'd like the stars to stay this kind. And two more squares behind my Wall, C21 and C22, so the north-east feeds itself whatever the next card says.

That extra ten isn't charity. As long as neither of your Land Deed Scrolls leaves the desert for Rich, or for anyone but me, the reader's pay stays at twenty every year I'm on the throne. If anyone makes you an offer for a Scroll, tell me the number first and I'll beat it from the crown.
Reina buys C21 and C22 for Province 1 (40, the crown). Salaries: Clark 10 as the Official, Rob 20 as the reader, doubled.

Where Years 9 and 10 leave the table: Reina is Empress with 52, after the Wall above Province 1, the Marble Pagoda and half of everyone's land; 400 of works are still owed (the Great Wall above Provinces 2 and 3, and the Province 3 Reservoir). Clark is the Official again with 191.5 and holds a Bowl; he needs a Land Deed and a Dragon Jar. Paddy, the Gentry, has 53.5 and needs only a Bowl. Rich, now the Silk Peasant, has 121 and holds a Customs House and a Bowl; he needs a Land Deed. Silke, the Rice Peasant, has 164.5 and nothing on the board. Rob has 157 and both Land Deeds in his desert, and needs a raided piece from Rich and from Silke.
The appointed reader's pay is the Empress's choice, not a debt she owes (an appointee is paid only if the Emperor chooses).

Utility Tax. A new levy, for the upkeep of things you may or may not have." Average harvest for everyone. Population holds at 400 million, so it's the x4 row on your tables. Every province pays the crown 2, and any province with a Public Works pays 2 more. Don't look at me, I haven't got any works, and I'm not paying tax on the ones I'm about to burn. Rich, W2 is one step from your Customs House. You'll want to pay for its upkeep quickly, while you've still got it.
Rob reads the Utility Tax: an average harvest everywhere, x4 holds; Provinces 2, 3, 5 and 6 each pay the Empress 2, and 2 more where they have a work (2, 5 and 6).

Storyteller's tip: there's no stock left, so every piece now changes hands by private trade. Both Land Deeds and one of the two Jars stand on Rob's desert, and he may sell them; Paddy holds the other Jar.

Paddy's own harvest is -85 and he has 53.5, so he sells his Customs House (M9) and Dragon Jar (M10) back to the Harvest Pile at 2 each before it pays out (Note 7). He is 27.5 in debt, 29.5 after the Utility Tax: no bids, trades, gifts of grain or seat change while it stands, and grain he receives pays it first. Both pieces are in the pile's stock and will be auctioned this year after the provinces' lots.

Rich, Silke, it's five each, same as always, and I'll not pretend I'm in a position to ask for more. Though if either of you fancied making it fifteen, with seven hundred and fifty and five hundred in your sacks, I'd remember it a long while. I sold my Jar and my Customs House back to the pile for two grain each tonight, the two pieces it took me four tries and a grain past careful to get, so I know exactly what being careful costs.
Rent: Rich and Silke pay Paddy 5 each, which goes to his debt (now 19.5). His hope of fifteen is a request each answers at their next turn.

Thirty percent, my friends, and not a grain more: Rich and Silke can carry it without noticing. The crown will build the whole of the Wall above Clark and Paddy this year and pay every link of it, three hundred and twenty, so neither of you owes me a single stone. Clark, your ten is safe, and Rob, your twenty is too, so long as our understanding stands. And Paddy, I'd hand you that fifteen myself if the rules let grain reach a man past his debt. Next year you'll have a Reservoir to show for your patience.

Reina declares 30% (291: Rich 190.5, Silke 100.5), will build all eight Wall links above Provinces 2 and 3 at the crown's whole cost (320), pays Clark 10 at year's end, and half of every square others buy.
A player in debt can't give grain, but anyone may give grain to one; it pays the debt first (Note 7).

Thirty percent, counted to the half: Rich, one hundred ninety and a half; Silke, one hundred and a half; Paddy and I owe nothing, and the book has us down for nothing. Two hundred ninety-one to the crown, Empress, every grain of it in the open, so nobody at this table can say the Official's thumb was on the scale. And Rob, I've written your refusal in ahead of time, saves us both the ink.

Clark collects 291 for the crown. Reina builds all eight Wall links above Provinces 2 and 3 (320, the crown). The strips below the Wall open for new land in Provinces 2 and 3. 80 of works are still owed: the Province 3 Reservoir.
Silke's set needs a Dragon Jar (with a Customs House and a Land Deed Scroll); only Rich doesn't need one.

The earliest the game can end is Year 12, not this year: one project a year, and this year's is the Wall. The Province 3 Reservoir (80) is the last work owed, so it can be built next year at the soonest, and land bought this year pays at least one harvest (Year 12's) before it does.

Empress, you've just walled me in at the crown's cost, and I'm grateful, so let me make the gift pay. Four squares under the new Wall, eighty to the pile: I'll put in twenty, and I'm asking the crown for sixty. That's cheap for an Official who'll still be able to afford an honest count next year, and the book has a very short page called 'Emperors who paid their Official well'. I'd like your name on it.
Clark asks for four squares under the new Wall, F12 to F15 (80): he'd pay 20 and asks the crown for 60, more than its half. The Empress answers after the other land asks.

Empress, the Wall is magnificent, and I'd never ask the crown for more than its customary half: four little squares at the far end of my coast, forty from me and forty from you, and the sea pays both of us back by next harvest. Paddy, my friend, the rent we agreed was five and five is what I've paid, to the grain. I'd only insult you by pretending a gift to your debt is anything but the pile's grain.
Rich buys four squares of sea, I28, J28, K29 and K30 (40 from him, 40 from the crown), and declines Paddy's extra 10 of rent.

Four squares at the far end of my sea, Empress, the customary half and not a grain more: forty from me, forty from you, and eighty back to the pile by next harvest. Paddy, five, same as every year, exactly as you taught me. And since everyone's counting: Rich, five hundred sixteen and a half; me, three-ninety, three-fifty after this; and there's a Customs House and a Jar in the pile with nobody's name on them yet.
Silke buys four squares, V27 to V30 (40 from her, 40 from the crown), and declines Paddy's extra 10 of rent.
